lessons.unit: Unit 2A: Component 2 or 3 Section A / Assignment A: Modern drama (choose one)
lessons.title: Modern drama: Component 3 assignment, critical style and personal engagement
lessons.bigQuestion: What does it take to write about a play with both control and a voice of your own?
objectives: State the Component 3 Assignment A rules: internally assessed, 30 marks (15 AO1, 15 AO2), externally moderated
Explain what the specification means by close understanding, critical style, informed personal engagement and use of examples
Write an analytical paragraph that shows all four qualities
successCriteria: All: state how many marks Assignment A carries and its AO split
Most: use an example and a personal judgement in each paragraph
Some: write in a critical style that argues a view, not just describes
lessons.crossCurricular: Drama and theatre studies; PSHE: independent study and deadlines
lessons.smsc: Moral and cultural: an honest personal response grounded in evidence

keywords.def: a task set and marked by the school, then moderated by the exam board
checking by the exam board that school marking is accurate
writing that argues, evaluates and explores a view
a considered, informed response of your own
a specific detail, moment or short quotation from the play
close knowledge of the text, critical style, informed personal engagement

starter: Bismillah. Name the two AOs for drama.
Give one reason why a writer might use a stage direction.

teach.heading: Two routes: Component 2 or Component 3
teach.note: Component 2 is an open-book exam. Component 3 is a non-examined alternative: two teacher-devised assignments (modern drama and literary heritage text), internally assessed and externally moderated. The specification gives the advisory length as 650 to 800 words each. Assignment A carries 30 marks: 15 for AO1 and 15 for AO2. Tell pupils that the school has not decided which route to run (check with the teacher in charge before planning).

left.title: Component 2 (exam)
points: Question from a choice of two

teach.heading: What AO1 asks for
teach.note: Teach the four ideas the specification stresses: close understanding of the play, a critical style, informed personal engagement and use of examples. Close understanding means accurate knowledge of events, characters and dramatic choices. Critical style means arguing a point, using tentative language ('suggests', 'invites') and weighing alternative readings. Personal engagement means a reasoned response, not 'I liked it'. Examples are precise moments or short quotations.
bullets: Informed personal engagement: your view, justified
Use examples: moment, line, stage direction

teach.heading: Model: a paragraph with all four qualities
teach.note: I do. Use An Inspector Calls as an example, with reference not long quotation. Show a paragraph: a clear argument, a precise example, a method (AO2) and a personal view.

model.problem: How does Priestley present responsibility in An Inspector Calls?
steps: Point (critical): Priestley argues that responsibility is shared, not private.
Example: the Inspector's final speech, where he warns that 'we are members of one body'.
Method (AO2): the Inspector's firm, direct address make the speech feel like a lesson to the audience as well as the family.
Personal engagement: I find this persuasive because the Birlings keep trying to escape blame, so the audience shares the Inspector's frustration.
model.answer: Priestley argues that responsibility is shared, not private. The Inspector's final speech, in which he warns that 'we are members of one body', is delivered directly and firmly, so it feels like a lesson to the audience as well as to the family. I find this persuasive because the Birlings keep trying to escape blame, which makes the audience share the Inspector's frustration.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. C is correct.

check.q: Which sentence shows informed personal engagement?
options: I liked the play.
The play is about a family.
The Inspector's pressing questions make the audience share his frustration, which I find persuasive because the Birlings keep avoiding blame.
Priestley was born in 1894.
check.why: C states a personal view and supports it with an example from the play. A has no evidence, B is only description and D is a fact about the writer, not engagement.

teach.heading: Writing for Component 3
teach.note: If the school uses Component 3, plan the assignment as a tight argument rather than a summary: one title, one clear line of argument, three or four examples with analysis, and a conclusion that states your view. Aim for the advisory 650 to 800 words, not more. Keep a log of your sources of help according to school rules.
bullets: Analysis of methods, not just plot

practice: Rewrite 'The play is about power' as a critical-style sentence.
Find one example from your set play that shows a method (stage direction, setting, speech).
Write one sentence of personal engagement on the play's ending.
independent: Core: write one paragraph with a point, an example, a method and your view.
Extend: write a paragraph that weighs two different interpretations of the same scene.
Stretch: plan a full 650-word response with an argument, four examples and a conclusion.
exit: State the marks and AO split for Assignment A.
Write one sentence in a critical style about your set play.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words on a question of your choice for your play, with one example, one method and one personal view.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a four-part paragraph frame. EAL: sentence starters for critical language. Stretch: introduce a literary critic's view in your own words (do not quote).

lessons.unit: Unit 2A-OPT: Modern drama options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Set plays: A View from the Bridge and An Inspector Calls
lessons.bigQuestion: How do two plays turn private choices into public judgments?
objectives: Summarise plot, setting and dramatic form of each play
Explain how each play presents responsibility, family and justice
Link each play to its context and dramatic methods
successCriteria: All: describe setting and main characters of each play
Most: explain how a dramatic method shows theme
Some: compare how each play uses a narrator-like figure to guide the audience
lessons.crossCurricular: History: 1950s New York and 1912 Edwardian England; Citizenship: law and responsibility

keywords.def: a play about a central figure whose flaw leads to downfall
a figure who comments on the action
the audience knows more than the characters
an instruction about action, setting or tone
unity of time, place and action
how a play is organised

starter: Bismillah. What is a stage direction?
Name one way a writer builds tension on stage.

teach.heading: A View from the Bridge: the basics
teach.note: Arthur Miller. First produced in 1955 as a one-act play, revised into two acts in 1956. Set in Red Hook, Brooklyn, among Italian-American dockworkers. Eddie Carbone, a longshoreman, and his wife Beatrice raise Beatrice's niece Catherine. When her cousins Marco and Rodolpho, illegal immigrants, arrive, Eddie's feelings for Catherine turn destructive. Alfieri, a lawyer, acts like a chorus, telling the story and warning of danger. Eddie's betrayal of the cousins to the immigration authorities breaks the community's code. The play is a modern tragedy.

teach.heading: An Inspector Calls: the basics
teach.note: J B Priestley, written in 1945, set in 1912 in the industrial city of Brumley. The prosperous Birling family are celebrating Sheila's engagement to Gerald Croft when Inspector Goole arrives to investigate the death of a young woman, Eva Smith, also known as Daisy Renton. Each family member is shown to have contributed to her suffering. The play is set in one room and unfolds in real time, in three acts. Priestley, a socialist, wrote after the Second World War, when Britain was building the welfare state; dramatic irony runs through Mr Birling's confident claims about the Titanic and war.
bullets: One room, continuous time, three acts
Eva Smith: the voice of the poor

teach.heading: Compare the two plays
teach.note: Use the table to prepare for a question on responsibility. Remind pupils to use stage directions and settings as evidence.

head: Feature
A View from the Bridge
An Inspector Calls
rows: Immigration; informing and loyalty in 1950s America
Class, welfare and war in 1912 and 1945

teach.heading: Model: dramatic method
teach.note: I do. Show how a stage direction or structural choice adds meaning. Use Alfieri's first speech as an example of narration and foreshadowing.

model.problem: How does Miller present Eddie's downfall as inevitable in A View from the Bridge?
steps: Point: Miller uses Alfieri to make Eddie's downfall feel fated.
Evidence: Alfieri opens by telling the audience that he saw the story's end coming, like a tragedy.
Zoom: this chorus-like narration creates dramatic irony, because we watch Eddie's choices already knowing where they lead.
Link: audience feels pity and fear, as in a Greek tragedy, which suits a play about an ordinary man brought down by his own flaw.
model.answer: Miller uses Alfieri to make Eddie's downfall feel fated. Alfieri tells the audience at the start that he saw the end coming, like a tragedy, so we watch Eddie's choices already knowing where they lead. This dramatic irony makes the audience feel pity and fear, as in a Greek tragedy, which suits a play about an ordinary man brought down by his own flaw.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. C is correct.

check.q: What is the main effect of Priestley's dramatic irony in Mr Birling's speeches about the Titanic and war?
options: It shows he is funny.
It tells the audience the play is set in the future.
It makes the audience doubt his judgment and the values he stands for.
It explains the plot.
check.why: The audience knows the later history, so Birling looks foolish. A, B and D misread the effect.

practice: Name one stage direction or setting detail in each play and say what it shows.
Explain who Alfieri and Inspector Goole are and how they guide us.
Say which play you think is more convincing about responsibility and why.
independent: Core: complete the comparison table with one example for each box.
Extend: write a paragraph on the role of Alfieri or the Inspector using an example and a method.
Stretch: compare how Miller and Priestley use setting to confine their characters.
exit: Name the setting and form of each play.
State one context point for each play.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words on 'How does the writer present responsibility?' for your play with one example and one method.
lessons.send: SEND: give a character map. EAL: pre-teach 'tragedy', 'chorus', 'irony'. Stretch: evaluate whether Eddie is a victim, a villain or both.

lessons.unit: Unit 2A-OPT: Modern drama options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Set plays: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time and Kindertransport
lessons.bigQuestion: How can staging make an audience see the world through someone else's mind?
objectives: Summarise plot, structure and staging of each play
Explain how each play presents family, truth and separation
Link each play to its context without over-claiming
successCriteria: All: describe the main characters and setting of each play
Most: explain how staging presents a point of view or two time periods
Some: compare how each play uses structure to reveal secrets
lessons.crossCurricular: Drama: physical theatre and staging; History: Kindertransport and the Second World War
lessons.smsc: Social: empathy for difference and for refugee children; Moral: honesty and trust

keywords.def: a work changed from one form to another
a structure that surrounds the main story
drama that uses movement and the body to tell the story
two time periods shown together
a person who flees danger
an object or character that stands for an idea

starter: Name one way a stage can show a character's thoughts.

teach.heading: Curious Incident: the basics
teach.note: Mark Haddon's 2003 novel, adapted for the stage by Simon Stephens (the play was first staged at the National Theatre in 2012; verify date). Christopher Boone, fifteen, lives in Swindon and loves maths. After he finds the neighbour's dog, Wellington, killed, he sets out to investigate and uncovers family secrets involving his father Ed and his mother Judy. His teacher Siobhan helps him write his account, which frames the play. The text does not name Christopher's condition: audiences see his behaviour and his way of seeing the world. The staging uses light, sound and movement to show how overwhelming the world can feel to him.

teach.heading: Kindertransport: the basics
teach.note: Diane Samuels, first staged 1993. The play moves between 1938-39 and the 1980s. Eva, a Jewish girl from Germany, is sent to Britain on the Kindertransport, which rescued around 10,000 mainly Jewish children from Nazi-controlled territories between November 1938 and September 1939. In Britain she becomes Evelyn, and her daughter Faith discovers the past. A figure called the Ratcatcher links to the Pied Piper story and to fear. Two time periods are shown together in one attic space, so past and present overlap on stage. Her German mother Helga and her English foster mother Lil represent two forms of motherhood.
bullets: Eva and Evelyn: one person, two lives
The Ratcatcher: fear and the Pied Piper

teach.heading: Staging and meaning
teach.note: Show how each play uses form. Curious Incident's staging takes us inside Christopher's mind; Kindertransport's overlapping timelines show how memory and identity are bound together. Ask pupils how an audience would feel if the past and present scenes appeared in separate rooms.

left.title: Curious Incident
points: Light, sound and movement show sensory overload

teach.heading: Model: staging as evidence
teach.note: I do. Use an overlapping scene in Kindertransport as an example of structure.

model.problem: How does Samuels use structure to explore identity in Kindertransport?
steps: Point: Samuels shows that Evelyn's past is still alive in the present.
Evidence: scenes from 1939 and the 1980s share the same attic space and sometimes overlap.
Zoom: the overlap suggests Evelyn cannot escape her earlier self, and Faith's discovery of the past makes the secret impossible to contain.
Link: for an audience that knows the history of the Kindertransport, the structure honours the child refugees' hidden grief.
model.answer: Samuels shows that Evelyn's past is still alive in the present. Scenes from 1939 and the 1980s share the same attic space and sometimes overlap, which suggests that Evelyn cannot escape her earlier self. Faith's discovery of the past makes the secret impossible to contain, and for an audience that knows the history of the Kindertransport, the structure honours the hidden grief of the child refugees.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: Why does Samuels set past and present in the same attic?
options: To save money on scenery.
To show that the past is still present in Evelyn's life.
To make the play shorter.
To avoid showing 1939.
check.why: B explains the dramatic effect. A, C and D are not supported by the play's meaning.

practice: Write one sentence on how each play is framed or structured.
Name one prop or staging detail in each play and what it represents.
Explain why the Ratcatcher is a useful figure for the audience.
independent: Core: complete a table of characters, setting and theme for each play.
Extend: write a paragraph on how staging helps the audience understand Christopher or Eva.
Stretch: compare how the two plays use framing and time to reveal secrets.
exit: Name the setting and time period of each play.
State one context point for each play.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words on 'How does the writer use staging?' for your play with one example and one method.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a character relationship map. EAL: pre-teach 'refugee', 'framing', 'adaptation'. Stretch: evaluate whether the play or the novel version of Curious Incident gives more insight (only if the novel has been read).

lessons.unit: Unit 2A-OPT: Modern drama options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Set play: Death and the King's Horseman, and the open-book rule for drama
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens when duty to a tradition and the pressure of an outside power collide?
objectives: Summarise plot, setting and structure of Death and the King's Horseman
Explain the main themes of duty, honour and cultural conflict
State the open-book rule for Component 2 modern drama: a clean, prescribed, unmarked edition (Appendix 3)
successCriteria: All: describe the main characters and the central ritual
Most: explain a theme with a stage example
Some: evaluate how Soyinka presents responsibility and cultural conflict
lessons.crossCurricular: History: British colonial rule in Nigeria; RE: ritual and duty
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: sacrifice, faith and the weight of duty; Moral: responsibility to others

keywords.def: a ceremony with fixed actions
the King's chief horseman, whose role includes accompanying the king in death
a performance with masks and costume
control of a country by a foreign power
something one is bound to do
a play about a central figure whose flaw leads to downfall

starter: Name one way a play can show a cultural difference.

teach.heading: The basics
teach.note: Wole Soyinka, Nigerian playwright and Nobel laureate (1986). The play is based on events in Oyo in 1946, in the period of British colonial rule. Elesin Oba, the King's Horseman, must die to accompany the King into the afterlife, but he delays and the District Officer Simon Pilkings intervenes. Elesin's son Olunde, trained as a doctor in England, returns to support his father's duty and takes his place. The market women and Iyaloja speak for the community. Soyinka says in his author's note that the play is not simply a clash of cultures (verify wording).

teach.heading: Dramatic features
teach.note: Soyinka draws on Yoruba oral tradition: song, praise-singing, drumming, dance and proverb. The market scene is full of music and movement, while the Pilkingses' house is formal and quiet. The egungun masquerade costume appears in a Pilkings' scene in contrast to the formal ball. These set contrasts help pupils write about staging. Remind pupils that in an open-book exam they can consult the play, so they need to know where to find key moments rather than memorise quotations.

teach.heading: Open-book rule and how to use it
teach.note: Component 2 is open book: pupils may take a clean prescribed edition of the play (paper or onscreen). Pearson publishes the permitted editions in Appendix 3; check the list before buying class sets. Unmarked means no annotations or highlighted notes. Teach tab-free fast scanning: know the structure by act or scene, so you can find evidence within seconds.

head: Open-book fact
Meaning for revision
rows: Check the Appendix 3 list before buying copies
No annotations, so notes must be in your head or planning sheet
Practise with whichever format you will use
Know where scenes are; do not copy long passages

teach.heading: Model: staging and theme
teach.note: I do. Take the contrast between the market and the Pilkings' house.

model.problem: How does Soyinka present the clash of values in Death and the King's Horseman?
steps: Point: Soyinka presents two worlds that cannot fully understand each other.
Evidence: the lively market scene and the formal colonial house, where Pilkings and Jane wear an egungun costume at a party.
Zoom: the sharp change of setting and the use of costume shows the colonial officers' misunderstanding of a sacred object.
Link: Soyinka does not reduce the play to a simple conflict; both Elesin and Pilkings share responsibility for the tragedy.
model.answer: Soyinka presents two worlds that cannot fully understand each other. The lively market scene contrasts with the formal colonial house, where the Pilkingses wear an egungun costume at a party, which shows how little the colonial officers understand a sacred object. Soyinka does not reduce the play to a simple conflict, because both Elesin and Pilkings share responsibility for the tragedy.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. A is correct.

check.q: What is true about the open-book Component 2 rule?
options: You may use a clean prescribed edition with no annotations.
You may bring your own annotated copy.
You may not bring the text.
You may bring any edition.
check.why: The specification requires a prescribed edition, unmarked. B, C and D are false.

practice: Say who each of these is: Elesin, Olunde, Iyaloja, Pilkings.
Name one staging contrast and say what it shows.
Explain 'unmarked edition' in your own words.
independent: Core: list five scenes with one line each so you can find them in the book.
Extend: write a paragraph on duty and honour using one example and one method.
Stretch: evaluate whether Elesin, Pilkings or neither is mostly responsible for the tragedy.
exit: State the setting and year of the play.
Give one rule about the book in Component 2.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words on 'How does Soyinka present duty?' with one example and one method; confirm the prescribed edition you will use.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a scene finder sheet. EAL: glossary for Yoruba terms. Stretch: compare to another play where duty conflicts with feeling.

lessons.unit: Unit 2B-OPT: Literary heritage options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Shakespeare for Component 2: Romeo and Juliet and The Merchant of Venice
lessons.bigQuestion: How does Shakespeare turn a conflict between groups into a human tragedy or a human question?
objectives: Summarise plot, setting and form of each play
Explain how each presents love, hatred, prejudice and justice
Link each play to its Elizabethan context in an AO4 sentence
successCriteria: All: describe the main characters and setting of each play
Most: explain a theme with a short quotation
Some: compare how each play ends and what that says about society
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Elizabethan England; RE: religious tolerance and justice
lessons.smsc: Moral: mercy, justice and prejudice; Social: love, family and conflict

keywords.def: a play where the central characters meet a sad end
a play with a happy ending, often with marriage
a 14-line poem; the prologue of Romeo and Juliet is one
the idea that events are decided in advance
an unfair opinion formed without good reason
a legal agreement

teach.heading: Romeo and Juliet: the basics
teach.note: Written around 1595 (approx.). Set in Verona. The feud between the Montagues and Capulets frames the play. The prologue is a sonnet that calls the lovers 'star-cross'd' and states the ending. Romeo and Juliet meet at a Capulet feast, marry in secret with the help of Friar Laurence, and die because of a chain of misunderstandings and haste. Key characters: Mercutio, Tybalt, the Nurse. Key contrasts: love and hate, youth and age, haste and patience. Friar Laurence warns 'Wisely and slow', but the plot rushes forward.

teach.heading: The Merchant of Venice: the basics
teach.note: Written around the mid-1590s (approx.). Set in Venice and Belmont. Antonio borrows money from the Jewish moneylender Shylock to help his friend Bassanio woo Portia. The bond is a pound of Antonio's flesh. Portia, disguised as a lawyer, appeals to 'the quality of mercy' and turns the law against Shylock. Context: Jews had been expelled from England in 1290 and Elizabethan audiences held negative stereotypes; Shylock's speech 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' asks for common humanity. Modern audiences debate whether the play endorses or criticises prejudice. Teach sensitively and link to wider respect for all faiths.
bullets: The bond: money, mercy and justice

teach.heading: Compare the two plays
teach.note: Use the table to prepare for a question on conflict. Discuss how each play ends, and who suffers.

teach.heading: Model: AO1, AO2 and AO4 in one paragraph
teach.note: I do. Use Shakespeare's prologue. Each AO appears within a single paragraph, in a mix.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare use the prologue of Romeo and Juliet to shape the audience's response?
steps: Point: the prologue makes the ending part of the audience's experience from the start.
Evidence: the lovers are called 'star-cross'd' and are said to take their lives.
Zoom: the sonnet form and the word 'star-cross'd' suggest fate, so the audience watches with dramatic irony.
Link: Elizabethan audiences were familiar with ideas of fortune and the stars, so the prologue positions the lovers as doomed.
model.answer: The prologue makes the ending part of the audience's experience from the start. The lovers are called 'star-cross'd' and are said to take their lives, and the sonnet form and the word 'star-cross'd' suggest fate, so the audience watches with dramatic irony. Elizabethan audiences were familiar with ideas of fortune and the stars, so the prologue positions the lovers as doomed.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: Which best explains why Shakespeare begins Romeo and Juliet with a sonnet prologue?
options: To confuse the audience.
To announce the tragic ending so that the audience watches with dramatic irony.
To introduce a comic subplot.
To show that Romeo is the hero.
check.why: B states the dramatic effect. A, C and D do not fit the prologue.

practice: Write the key setting and genre of each play.
Find one theme in each play and one short quotation to support it.
Say why context matters differently for each play.
independent: Core: complete the comparison table with a scene reference in each box.
Extend: write a paragraph on conflict in your chosen play using AO1, AO2 and AO4.
Stretch: evaluate how far Shakespeare invites sympathy for Shylock or for the feuding families.
exit: Name the genre of each play.
State one context point for each play.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word paragraph on conflict in your chosen play with one quotation (max five words), one method and one context point.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a scene summary sheet. EAL: glossary of Elizabethan words. Stretch: explore how modern productions might change the audience's response.

lessons.unit: Unit 2B-OPT: Literary heritage options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Heritage prose: Pride and Prejudice and Great Expectations
lessons.bigQuestion: What do two nineteenth-century novels tell us about money, class and how people change?
objectives: Summarise plot, setting and narration of each novel
Explain how each presents class, marriage or ambition and personal growth
Use context in a short AO4 sentence
successCriteria: All: describe the main characters and setting of each novel
Most: explain a theme with a short quotation or reference
Some: compare how each writer uses narration to guide the reader
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Regency and Victorian society; Economics: inheritance and wealth

keywords.def: saying one thing and meaning another, or a gap between expectation and reality
narration that blends the narrator's voice with a character's thoughts
a narrator looking back on past events
a legal rule that passes an estate to a male heir
a group of people with a similar position in society
a novel about growing up and learning

starter: What is the difference between first-person and third-person narration?
Name two kinds of context in AO4.

teach.heading: Pride and Prejudice: the basics
teach.note: Jane Austen, published in 1813. Set in rural England among the gentry. The Bennets of Longbourn have five daughters and an estate that will pass by entail to a male cousin, Mr Collins, so the daughters need to marry well. Elizabeth Bennet's quick judgment of Mr Darcy at first meeting is shaped by pride and prejudice on both sides. The famous opening ironically claims a rich single man must want a wife. The narrator is third person with a witty, ironic tone and often shares Elizabeth's viewpoint. Key plot: Netherfield, Wickham and Lydia, Darcy's first proposal (verify chapter number) and Pemberley. Context: marriage as economic security for women in Regency England.
bullets: Irony and wit in the narration

teach.heading: Great Expectations: the basics
teach.note: Charles Dickens, published in weekly instalments in 1860-61 (approx.). Pip, an orphan raised by his sister and her kind husband Joe Gargery, is invited to Miss Havisham's decaying house and falls in love with Estella. He receives money from an unknown benefactor and moves to London to become a gentleman. He later learns the benefactor is the convict Magwitch. Pip narrates as an older man, looking back with regret. The novel has three stages of Pip's expectations. Dickens' own experience of childhood poverty and class snobbery shapes the novel. Context: Victorian ideas of what makes a gentleman.

teach.heading: Compare: narration and class
teach.note: Use the table. Ask how each writer judges class snobbery. Austen's irony teases; Dickens' retrospective voice judges.

head: Feature
Pride and Prejudice
Great Expectations
rows: Third person, ironic, close to Elizabeth
First person, Pip as older man
Chastened Pip; ending revised from first version (verify)

teach.heading: Model: narration and context
teach.note: I do. Use the opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice.

model.problem: How does Austen use the opening of Pride and Prejudice to introduce her themes?
steps: Point: Austen uses irony to expose the novel's concern with marriage and money.
Evidence: the first sentence says it is a 'truth universally acknowledged' that a wealthy bachelor needs a wife.
Zoom: the confident tone is ironic, because it is the families who need rich husbands, not the men who need wives.
Link: in Regency England, women had few ways to gain security, so marriage was an economic matter, which is the pressure that shapes the Bennets.
model.answer: Austen uses irony to expose the novel's concern with marriage and money. The first sentence calls it a 'truth universally acknowledged' that a wealthy bachelor needs a wife, but the confident tone is ironic, because it is families with daughters who need rich husbands. In Regency England women had few ways to gain security, so marriage was an economic matter, which is the pressure that shapes the Bennets.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. C is correct.

check.q: Why is Pip's retrospective narration important in Great Expectations?
options: It means Pip has never made mistakes.
It removes all emotion.
It lets the older Pip judge his younger self with regret.
It tells the story in the present tense.
check.why: C explains the effect: hindsight allows judgment. A, B and D misdescribe the narrator.

practice: Write one sentence for each novel stating its setting and narrator.
Name one flaw in each protagonist.
Say how the context of money affects each novel.
independent: Core: complete the comparison table with a scene or quotation (up to five words) in each box.
Extend: write a paragraph on narration in your chosen novel.
Stretch: argue which novel is more critical of class.
exit: State one context point for each novel.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words on class in your chosen novel with one quotation (max five words), one method and one context point.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a character map. EAL: glossary of period terms. Stretch: compare with another novel you know about class.

teach.heading: The basics
teach.note: Nathaniel Hawthorne, published in 1850. Set in a Puritan community in 17th-century Boston, Massachusetts. Hester Prynne is forced to wear a scarlet letter 'A' for adultery and to bear her daughter Pearl alone. The father, the minister Arthur Dimmesdale, hides his guilt. Hester's husband, Roger Chillingworth, seeks revenge. The scaffold appears at the start, middle and end. Hawthorne's own ancestor was a judge in the Salem witch trials, which informs his view of Puritan severity. The novel opens with 'The Custom-House', a sketch about how the writer claims to have found the story (verify chapter details).

teach.heading: Symbolism and themes
teach.note: The letter A begins as a mark of shame, but as Hester lives with it and helps others, many in the town begin to read it differently, and Hawthorne leaves it open to interpretation. Pearl is both a living reminder and a symbol of nature and freedom. Themes: sin and guilt, public punishment and private suffering, truth, and the cruelty or mercy of society. Literary context: Romanticism and American allegory.
bullets: Pearl: symbol of nature and truth

teach.heading: Open-book revision
teach.note: Component 2 is open book: a clean prescribed edition is allowed (paper or onscreen) and Appendix 3 lists several per text, so check which edition you have before the exam. Unmarked means no notes in the book. Prepare a quick-find map: parts or chapters, key events, character moments. Practise finding a passage in under thirty seconds. Never copy long passages: the marks are for analysis and context.

model.problem: How does Hawthorne use the scaffold to present public judgment in The Scarlet Letter?
steps: Point: Hawthorne uses the scaffold to show how the community punishes in public.
Evidence: Hester stands on it at the start, Dimmesdale at night in the middle, and both at the end.
Zoom: its repeated use structures the novel and shows how guilt is public for Hester but hidden for Dimmesdale.
Link: Puritan society judged sin harshly, and Hawthorne, whose ancestor was a judge at Salem, questions that severity.
model.answer: Hawthorne uses the scaffold to show how the community punishes in public. Hester stands on it at the start, Dimmesdale at night in the middle, and both at the end, which structures the novel and shows that guilt is public for Hester but hidden for Dimmesdale. Puritan society judged sin harshly, and Hawthorne, whose ancestor was a judge at Salem, questions that severity.

teach.heading: What the Pearson question rewards
teach.note: Pearson Component 2 Section B: one 30-mark question from a choice of two, assessed 10 AO1, 10 AO2 and 10 AO4, and the exam is open book with a clean prescribed edition (verify the exact question wording in the sample assessment material). The mark balance is equal across three AOs, so context carries real marks. Macbeth is on the Pearson literary heritage list. If pupils have practised closed-book, extract-based questions elsewhere, point out that here they choose their own evidence from the whole play.

teach.note: I do. Use the dagger soliloquy. The paragraph mixes a view, a method and a context link.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth's guilt before and after the murder of Duncan?
steps: Point (AO1): Shakespeare presents guilt as something that begins in Macbeth's imagination before the crime.
Evidence: 'Is this a dagger which I see before me', a hallucination at 2.1.
Zoom (AO2): the question form and the vision suggest a mind torn and fevered; the soliloquy form lets the audience see his conscience at work.
Context (AO4): Jacobean audiences believed regicide was a crime against God, so Macbeth's mental torment would seem proper punishment for killing an anointed king.
model.answer: Shakespeare presents guilt as something that begins in Macbeth's imagination before the crime. The hallucination 'Is this a dagger which I see before me' is phrased as a question, which suggests a mind torn and fevered, and the soliloquy lets the audience watch his conscience at work. Jacobean audiences believed that killing an anointed king was a crime against God, so Macbeth's mental torment would have seemed a fitting punishment.
